utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, and Dragoljub Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, Geoffrey Nice, Christina Romano, Milbert Shin, Christina Mueller, Patricia Fikirini, and our case manager is Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Eugene O'Sullivan appearing on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Toma Fila and I represent Mr. Sainovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I am Tomislav Visnjic for the Defence of General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. We have a number of matters to get through today, and I'll begin with motions that are pending. We have two Prosecution motions to vary nondisclosure orders. The motions were filed in December, and a response was filed by the Ojdanic Defence. No other responses have been filed. And I am to say that the Chamber will give a decision on that motion shortly. There is the Ojdanic motion challenging jurisdiction over events in Kosovo, and I'm referring here to the appeal from the decision of the Trial Chamber in that matter. And that is still before the Appeals Chamber. I understand that the Appeals Chamber will shortly be adopting a particular decision in relation to this matter, which is very important for the progress in the pre-trial proceedings. I say it's important because on it hangs a number of other things, the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, which is to be filed one month after that decision, and then, of course, the Defence pre-trial briefs. Disclosure of witness statements, disclosure made under Rule 66 (A)(i) and 66(A)(ii). There was a matter, Mr. Nice, in relation to two witnesses to whom protective measures had been extended. The Prosecution has dropped one, I understand, but there was one other in relation to which a report was to be made on a monthly basis. One report was filed 21st November, and none has been filed since. So one is now due.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, there has been no change in the circumstances. Efforts have been made to pursue the circumstances of that particular witness and see what they are, but it's very difficult. The present report will be to the same effect, I think, as the report in November. It can, of course, be filed. But there are active steps to see what further moves, if any, may be made so far as that witness is concerned. At the hearing two days ago, we made the point to Senior Legal Officer Featherstone that the consequences of the order for us is that witnesses are having to be dropped because of difficulties over disclosure at this very early stage in the trial because whatever the Appeals Chamber's decision may be, there's quite a long time to go even before the earliest 65 ter date at which witness lists would normally become appropriate. And we regret that we had to drop one witness. So far as the other one is concerned, we're doing our best to see how much further we can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Expert witnesses, expert reports have been disclosed, both in B/C/S and in English. Rule 68 disclosure, there were some amendments to the Rules recently. There is now an obligation on the Defence in relation to certain matters, and the Prosecution still has some responsibility. Mr. Nice, anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, nothing, again, save beyond what I said in the presence of Ms. Featherstone the other day. The working out -- the practical working out of these changes in the Rules may, of course, take some time. There may be some further clarification or refinement of the Rules that will eventually be required. But we recognise both our continuing obligation as well as the fact that we have been relieved in part the obligation that previously existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, your basic requirement now is to pass over to the Defence certain material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In our actual knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In your actual knowledge, yes. And the rest to be made available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. When the electronic suite, as it's so described, is fully operational, then of course the Defence have access to a substantial majority of the overall collection of the OTP. Our duties in relation to the balance are determined by the phrase "actual knowledge," a phrase not yet further defined or identified. I think I can probably speak for this case and for others in saying that we will be cautious before abandoning practices that operated in favour of the accused too extensively. I mean we will be cautious before we abandon them too extensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a phrase that's unfamiliar to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but I have yet to be quite sure what it means in this context. But yes, we are aware of the changes and we are doing our best to ensure that we comply with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any remarks from the Defence counsel on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Not on this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Reciprocal disclosure, I understand, there's no particular problem. Does anyone wish to make any comment on that? No. There's disclosure from the Milosevic trial. Some difficulties had been encountered, but I understand that they have been resolved. Agreed and adjudicated facts. At the last conference, Mr. Fila, you were told to make a list of agreed facts, to pass them over to the Prosecution. Where are you with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Monday, this list was given to Mr. Nice, and now I have met my obligations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many facts on the list? Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We received this document two days ago of 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it says 17, but it may be that it's 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought there were 18, but it's 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we have in mind the following, that the first effort to agree facts was built on the indictment by the Prosecution inviting Defence could agree to parts of the indictment, which seems to us the way in which these -- the issues between the parties might be narrowed down. That was rejected, and a counterproposal was made, and Your Honour said on the last occasion, I think it was, that the Sainovic Defence team's proposal of a different methodology, that is, a list of facts which go beyond the statement-by-statement approach in relation to the indictment was one that you thought to be reasonable. So that what's been offered has been offered on the basis that it goes beyond the statement-by-statement approach in relation to the indictment. What we have been provided with is, we regret to say, we think entirely inappropriate and of very little or probably no value. The first series of facts relate to matters of history or constitutions that preceded that which is relevant for the indictment, and the latter half-dozen or so raise the sort of self-evidently contentious statement such as the following: "The degree of self-governance of Kosovo and Metohi [phoen] For the period 1968 until 1998 was larger than the degree of autonomy of the federal units in some federations, for example, Austria, Canada, and India." A proposition with or without a factual basis that would be hard for a Trial Chamber, I think, to handle valuably. And also, doesn't appear to be, if I may diffidently say so, doesn't appear to be responsive in any way to parts of the indictment, and really agreed facts are only going to be of value if they specifically address by one means or another either the indictment or the pre-trial brief, which are the documents that identify the Prosecution's case. Typically, just to make the point obvious, although I'm sure it is, in a domestic case of theft of property from Mr. AB, a defendant could admit that yes, the property was the property of Mr. AB. And then the question is whether the defendant stole it, something like that. And where the Sainovic Defence proposed this methodology beyond that which had been rejected and that was indictment-related, we fear that they have rather failed to meet up to the promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, be that as it may. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the methodology which we suggested was used in the Omarska case. We received a proposal, a point-by-point proposal from the Prosecution. We accepted what we accepted. And on our part we proposed some things, some of which the Prosecution accepted. The methodology which we proposed, I think there were 16 or 17 points, so I would expect the Prosecution to respond in writing what of those points they accept and which ones they don't. I do not ask for an evaluation of what is reasonable of those and what is not, because there must be a reason why we're proposing them. So the Prosecution should say "we are accepting this, and we are not accepting this" just as we will do the same to them. I will not put forth any opinion about what Mr. Nice is suggesting, whether it is wise or not. So this is what I'm expecting from the Prosecution. If they agree, fine. And if they don't agree, that is also fine. That is up to them. So this is as much as I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The exercise should be continued in good faith, and the Trial Chamber is available to assist if there are difficulties. 92 bis, the discussions on this are probably premature at this time. The Prosecution witness list still hasn't been served. And as I said earlier, much depends on the Appeals Chamber's decision coming out shortly in the Ojdanic jurisdictional matter. The other matter is the length of trial, and there was an original estimate of 100 to 120 witnesses with the trial taking perhaps three to four months. I wonder, is there any matter that any of the counsel would wish to raise? Any specific matter? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is a matter I would like to address at some point in this conference in relation to conditions of detention. I'm not sure if you want to deal with that at the end or now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, now, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next conference has to be held before Friday, the 21st of May. And I'm going to set Wednesday, May 12th. That’s some time away. If there is to be any change, the parties will be notified. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: adjourned at 3.40 p.m.
